title: Curie-Weiss cell fluid model: Fitting to experimental critical-point data
authors: I. V. Pylyuk, O. A. Dobush, M. P. Kozlovskii, R. V. Romanik, M. A. Shpot
abstract: We examine how the Curie--Weiss cell fluid model can be quantitatively related to real fluids by determining its microscopic parameters from experimental critical-point data for water, carbon dioxide, and three polyol ester lubricants (POE5, POE7, and POE9). The microscopic parameters of the model are determined from the experimental values of the critical temperature and critical density: the global attraction coupling constant is fixed by the critical temperature, and the cell volume by the critical density. The critical pressure then follows as an independent model prediction, deviating from experimental values by 10--41$\%$ across the studied substances. Varying the ratio of local repulsion to global attraction $f=J_2/J_1$ over a wide range has only a weak effect on this deviation. For $f\geq1$, the model's critical compressibility factor lays within a narrow range $Z_c\approx0.382-0.386$, remaining close to the mean-field van der Waals value $Z_c=3/8=0.375$ and consistently overestimating experimental values. The best agreement with experiment is obtained for the polyol ester lubricants and improves along the POE5--POE7--POE9 series with increasing molar mass, suggesting that multiple-occupancy cell fluid models are well suited to systems of large molecules, particularly soft-matter systems with bounded interaction potentials. We further show that generalizing the model by introducing a temperature- and phase-dependent effective attraction allows it to describe a triple point and to reproduce the broad range of critical-to-triple temperature ratios $T_c/T_{\mathrm{tr}}$ characteristic of real fluids.
summary: This paper applies the Curie-Weiss cell fluid model to analyze the critical and triple-point behavior of various real fluids. By fitting the model's microscopic parameters to experimental critical data, the authors demonstrate that the model provides a good description, particularly for large molecules, and can be successfully extended to describe complex phase coexistence regions.
main_problem: To establish a quantitative link between the microscopic parameters of the Curie-Weiss cell fluid model and the macroscopic critical and triple-point data of real fluids.
main_result: The model shows the best agreement with experimental data for polyol ester lubricants, suggesting its suitability for soft-matter systems, and can be generalized to describe the triple point region.
method: The authors fit the model's microscopic parameters ($J_1, v$) by matching the model's predictions for the critical temperature and density to experimental values.
model_or_system: The study uses the Curie-Weiss cell fluid model, characterized by global attraction ($J_1$) and local repulsion ($J_2$), applied to real fluids like water, $	ext{CO}_2$, and polyol ester lubricants.
key_observables: Critical temperature ($T_c$), critical density ($ho_c$), critical pressure ($P_c$), critical compressibility factor ($Z_c$), and the ratio $T_c/T_{tr}$.
important_parameters: The ratio of local repulsion to global attraction ($f=J_2/J_1$), and the temperature- and phase-dependent attraction parameters ($\alpha_\pi$).
main_assumptions: The model relies on a mean-field approximation, and initial parameter fitting is done using only the critical point data, requiring generalization to address the triple point.
figures_summary: The notes mention figures illustrating the phase diagram with coexistence lines and the comparison of model predictions versus experimental data for critical and triple points.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the model parameters using critical point data, noting deviations in $P_c$ and $Z_c$. It then generalizes the model by introducing temperature-dependent attraction to successfully describe the triple point and reproduce the range of $T_c/T_{tr}$ observed in real fluids.
why_interesting: While focused on classical fluids, the methodology of parameterizing complex many-body interactions (like the Curie-Weiss term) and mapping them onto measurable macroscopic phase transitions is relevant for developing effective Hamiltonians in quantum many-body systems.
